title: Slander
hook: spreading falsehood that harms a name

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: rechilut, carrying tales. Your line was don't carry tales. Did a tale reach you, and did it stop with you? Today, a harm that's heavier because it isn't even true. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

Who started it? By the fourth telling, nobody can say. A parent at school pickup sees a for-sale sign on a family's lawn and wonders aloud whether they're in trouble with money. The next parent repeats it as a fact. By Friday the family is losing the house. None of it happened. They're moving to be closer to a grandmother who needs help. But the story has a life of its own now, and the true version never seems to travel as fast. The last few days have been about harmful speech that is true. Jewish teaching has a separate name, and a heavier one, for harmful speech that is false. That name is today's word.
screen: `A FOR-SALE SIGN.` → `A GUESS BECOMES A FACT.` → `THE TRUTH TRAVELS SLOWER.`

segments.voice: Motzi shem ra. Word for word, bringing out a bad name. Turn it four ways. First, it's the Torah's own phrase. In Deuteronomy a man turns against his new wife and invents an accusation against her, and the text says he "hath brought up an evil name" on her. The law there takes her side. The lie is treated as an injury, and he is the one who pays for it. A name, in this picture, is something that can be wounded. Second, where it sits among the other kinds of speech. Teachers of Jewish ethics, the Chafetz Chaim among them, draw a line. Lashon hara is a hurtful thing that's true. Motzi shem ra is a hurtful thing that's false. The first is already forbidden, even though it's accurate. The second adds a lie to the harm, and tradition counts it heavier. Third, the commandment behind it. Among the Ten Commandments: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." Some readers hear that only in a courtroom. The teachers of speech hear it at the kitchen table too, because a rumor is testimony with no judge to check it. Fourth, the small versions. A false name doesn't need a whole invention. A guess passed along as fact. A detail dropped that would have changed the story. "I heard she..." with nothing behind it. And because a false story keeps moving after it leaves you, Jewish teaching on repentance asks for more than going quiet. It asks for repair: going back, as far as you can reach, and setting it straight. That's harder than silence. It's also the one thing that goes after the story once it has left.
screen: `BRINGING OUT A BAD NAME.` · `TRUE HARM, OR FALSE HARM.` · `NO FALSE WITNESS, EVEN AT HOME.` · `REPAIR, NOT JUST SILENCE.` · then, large: `NO FALSE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: correct one false story. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few weeks for one thing you said, passed along, or let stand that turned out to be wrong about someone. It may be small: a guess about why a friend canceled, a story about a coworker you never checked. Who heard it from you? See that person's face. Now find the plain sentence that would set it straight. "I said that, and I was wrong." Say it once, silently. If nothing comes to mind, think of a false story going around about someone, and what one true sentence in its place would sound like. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for the nerve to say it out loud. The bell holds the time.
Motzi shem ra. Bringing out a bad name: harmful speech that is also false. The phrase comes from Deuteronomy itself. Today's word.
Your line: no false names. Today, set one false story straight with someone who heard it from you, in a single plain sentence. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on speech distinguishes lashon hara, hurtful truth, from motzi shem ra, hurtful falsehood; repentance for it is understood to include repairing the harm, not only stopping.

Exodus 20:13 is the JPS 1917 verse number for 'bear false witness' (KJV 20:16); confirm.
The distinction lashon hara (true) vs motzi shem ra (false), and that motzi shem ra is graver, is attributed to the Chafetz Chaim and 'tradition'; confirm.
